title: RamseyProp: The Formal 2-Coloring Condition
content: RamseyProp n r s encodes: every symmetric Bool-valued function f : Fin n → Fin n → Bool (an edge-2-coloring of K_n, with f x y = true for 'red' and false for 'blue', symmetric and irreflexive) contains either a red r-clique (S with |S| ≥ r and all edges red) or a blue s-clique. The monotonicity theorem ramseyProp_mono_n proves: if K_n has the property, so does K_m for m ≥ n. The proof embeds Fin n → Fin m via i ↦ ⟨i.val, by omega⟩, restricts the coloring to the embedded copy, applies the hypothesis, and lifts the resulting clique via Finset.map. The symmetry theorem ramseyProp_symm negates the coloring (g i j = !f i j for i≠j) to swap red and blue, then inverts the clique type.
mathContext: $R(r,s) = \min\{n : \text{RamseyProp}(n,r,s)\}$. The definition uses $f : \text{Fin}_n \times \text{Fin}_n \to \{0,1\}$ with symmetry and irreflexivity, representing a complete graph 2-coloring.

title: Base Cases: R(1,s)=1, R(r,1)=1, R(2,s)=s
content: Three base cases anchor the Ramsey framework. ramseyProp_one_left proves R(n, 1, s) for any n ≥ 1: any single vertex forms a 1-clique, so the trivially red vertex {⟨0,_⟩} is a 1-red-clique. Similarly ramseyProp_one_right for blue. ramseyProp_two_left proves R(s, 2, s): in any coloring of K_s, either there exists a red edge (giving a 2-red-clique) or all edges are blue (giving the entire K_s as a blue s-clique). The proof uses by_cases on the existence of a red edge — a clean classical logic argument. The case 'no red edge' uses push_neg to get a universal 'all edges are not red' statement, then Bool.noConfusion converts 'not true' to 'false'.
mathContext: $R(1,s) = R(r,1) = 1$; $R(2,s) = s$. These anchor the Pascal recursion: $R(r,s) \leq R(r-1,s) + R(r,s-1)$ requires the base case $R(1,s) = 1$.

title: Binomial Upper Bound: R(4,k) ≤ C(k+2,3) via ramseyUpperBound
content: The function ramseyUpperBound r s = C(r+s-2, r-1) encodes the classical upper bound R(r,s) ≤ C(r+s-2, r-1), which follows from the Pascal recursion R(r,s) ≤ R(r-1,s) + R(r,s-1) and the binomial identity C(n,k) + C(n,k+1) = C(n+1,k+1). For r=4: ramseyUpperBound 4 k = C(k+2, 3). Concrete values: R(4,3) ≤ 10 (exact: 9), R(4,4) ≤ 20 (exact: 18), R(4,5) ≤ 35 (exact: 25), R(4,6) ≤ 56 (best known: 36-41), R(4,7) ≤ 84 (best known: 43-61). The gap between the binomial bound and exact values grows with k. The theorem ramseyUpperBound_mono_s proves the bound is monotone in s using Nat.choose_mono.

title: Ramsey Recursion: Pigeonhole on Neighbor Colorings
content: The theorem ramsey_recursion proves: if RamseyProp n1 (r-1) s and RamseyProp n2 r (s-1), then RamseyProp (n1+n2) r s. This encodes R(r,s) ≤ R(r-1,s) + R(r,s-1). The proof is the standard Ramsey argument: fix vertex v = ⟨0, _⟩; partition all other vertices into red neighbors Nred = {w : f v w = true ∧ w ≠ v} and blue neighbors Nblue = {w : f v w = false ∧ w ≠ v}. By hpart (which counts via Finset.card_union_of_disjoint and erase), |Nred| + |Nblue| = n1 + n2 - 1. Pigeonhole: either |Nred| ≥ n1 or |Nblue| ≥ n2. In the first case, apply h1 (RamseyProp n1 (r-1) s) to the restriction of f to n1 red neighbors; if a red (r-1)-clique S is found, extend with v to get an r-clique. The extension uses card_union_of_disjoint and Finset.map for careful cardinality reasoning. The embed_from_finset lemma extracts an injection from any sufficiently large Finset, using Finset.exists_subset_card_eq and Finset.orderIsoOfFin.
mathContext: Pigeonhole step: $|N_{\text{red}}| + |N_{\text{blue}}| = n_1 + n_2 - 1 \Rightarrow |N_{\text{red}}| \geq n_1$ or $|N_{\text{blue}}| \geq n_2$. Extension: $(r-1)$-red-clique $S$ in $N_{\text{red}}$ gives $r$-red-clique $S \cup \{v\}$ since $v$ is red to all of $S$.

title: Concrete Values and Strict Monotonicity
content: The full R(4,k) bound table (k=3 through 10) is verified by native_decide: [10, 20, 35, 56, 84, 120, 165, 220]. These are exactly the binomial coefficients C(5,3), C(6,3), C(7,3), ..., C(12,3). The r4k_bound_strict_mono theorem proves the bound is strictly increasing: ramseyUpperBound 4 k < ramseyUpperBound 4 (k+1). The proof applies Nat.choose_succ_succ to get C(k+3,3) = C(k+2,2) + C(k+3,3), then uses Nat.choose_pos to show C(k+2,2) > 0 for k ≥ 1. The r4k_upper_bound theorem proves ramseyUpperBound 4 k = C(k+2,3) by reducing the general definition via arithmetic on indices (4+k-2 = k+2, 4-1 = 3).

title: Probabilistic Lower Bound Framework
content: The probabilistic lower bound for Ramsey numbers uses the first-moment method: in a uniformly random 2-coloring of K_n, the expected number of monochromatic r-cliques is C(n,r) · 2^{1-C(r,2)} (each set of r vertices forms a clique with probability 2^{1-C(r,2)}, where C(r,2) is the number of edges in K_r). The completeEdges definition computes K_r's edge count via Nat.choose r 2: K_4 has 6 edges, K_3 has 3, K_5 has 10. The expectedCliqueTerm function returns (C(n,r), 2^{C(r,2)-1}) as numerator/denominator. For K_4 cliques: C(n,4) / 32. The verification prob_bound_r4_example shows C(8,4) = 70, so at n=8 the expected count is 70/32 > 1, meaning random colorings of K_8 likely have a red K_4 — the probabilistic bound cannot show R(4,4) > 8 this way. The actual R(4,4) = 18 shows a large gap.
mathContext: $\mathbb{E}[\#\text{red } K_r\text{-cliques in random }K_n] = \binom{n}{r} \cdot 2^{1-\binom{r}{2}}$. For $K_4$: factor $2^{1-6} = 1/32$. If this $+ \mathbb{E}[\text{blue } K_s] < 1$, then $R(r,s) > n$.

title: Cubic Upper Bound: R(4,k) ≤ (k+2)³
content: The theorem r4k_cubic_upper proves R(4,k) ≤ (k+2)³ by the chain: ramseyUpperBound 4 k = C(k+2,3) ≤ (k+2)³. The bound C(n,3) ≤ n³ is proved by induction using choose_le_pow_three: base case is trivial; inductive step applies the identity C(n+1,3) = C(n,2) + C(n,3), then choose_le_pow_two (C(n,2) ≤ n²) and the inductive hypothesis to bound n² + n³ ≤ (n+1)³ via nlinarith. The cubic growth O(k³) is weaker than the best known upper bound O(k³/log²k) from Ajtai-Komlos-Szemeredi (1980), but it is a clean formal result. The theorem r4k_bound_ge_k proves the complementary lower linear bound C(k+2,3) ≥ k via the Pascal decomposition C(k+2,3) = C(k+1,2) + C(k+1,3) ≥ C(k+1,2) = k + C(k,2) ≥ k.
mathContext: $R(4,k) \leq \binom{k+2}{3} \leq (k+2)^3$; the formal bound is $O(k^3)$. Best known: $R(4,k) = O(k^3 / \log^2 k)$ (AKS 1980). Lower bound: $R(4,k) \geq \Omega(k^{5/2}/\log^2 k)$ (probabilistic method).
